facts.statement: Dromaeosauroides is a genus of dromaeosaurid dinosaur.
facts.quote: taxon: Dromaeosauroides

facts.statement: The genus Dromaeosauroides was named by Christiansen and Bonde in 2003.
facts.quote: authority: Christiansen & Bonde, 2003

facts.statement: Dromaeosauroides lived during the Early Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Early Cretaceous,

facts.statement: Fossils of Dromaeosauroides have been found in what is now Denmark and possibly England.
facts.quote: Dromaeosauroides is a genus of dromaeosaurid dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous of what is now Denmark and possibly also England.

facts.statement: The first remains of Dromaeosauroides were discovered in the Jydegaard Formation on the island of Bornholm.
facts.quote: It was discovered in the Jydegaard Formation in the Robbedale valley, on the island of Bornholm in the Baltic Sea.

facts.statement: Dromaeosauroides is the first and only scientifically named dinosaur known from Denmark.
facts.quote: Dromaeosauroides is the first known dinosaur from Denmark, and the only one which has been scientifically named.

facts.statement: Dromaeosauroides is one of the oldest known dromaeosaurs and the first uncontested dromaeosaur from the Early Cretaceous of Europe.
facts.quote: It is one of the oldest known dromaeosaurs in the world, and the first known uncontested dromaeosaur from the Early Cretaceous of Europe.

facts.statement: Dromaeosauroides is known from two teeth found in 2000 and 2008.
facts.quote: It is known from two teeth, the first of which was found in 2000 and the second in 2008.

facts.statement: The genus name means "Dromaeosaurus-like" and the species name means "from Bornholm".
facts.quote: The genus name means "Dromaeosaurus-like", due to the similarity to the teeth of that genus, and the species name means "from Bornholm".

facts.statement: The holotype tooth was certified as "Danekræ" (Danish creature) due to its scientific importance.
facts.quote: The first tooth was certified "Danekræ" ("Danish creature") when its scientific importance was evaluated.

facts.statement: The teeth of Dromaeosauroides are curved and finely serrated.
facts.quote: They are curved and finely serrated.

facts.statement: Dromaeosauroides was approximately 2 to 3 meters long and weighed about 40 kg.
facts.quote: In life, Dromaeosauroides would have been 2 to 3 m in length, and weighed about 40 kg.

facts.statement: Studies suggest dromaeosaurs used their sickle claws to grasp prey while dismembering them with their mouths.
facts.quote: 21st-century studies suggest they used them to grasp and restrain struggling prey while dismembering them with the mouth.

facts.statement: Dromaeosauroides lived in a coastal lagoon environment alongside sauropods.
facts.quote: Dromaeosauroides lived in a coastal lagoon environment with sauropods, as evidenced by a possible titanosaur tooth.

facts.statement: The first tooth was found during a field course taught by Christiansen and Bonde in September 2000.
facts.quote: In September 2000, Danish palaeontologists Per Christiansen and Niels Bonde taught a field course at the site, "The Hunt for Danish Dinosaurs".

facts.statement: A geology student named Eliza Jarl Estrup found the first dinosaur tooth on Danish territory during a field course.
facts.quote: During the course, geology student Eliza Jarl Estrup found a theropod tooth, the first dinosaur discovered on Danish territory, and the find was recorded by a local television station.

facts.statement: The holotype tooth was catalogued as MGUH 27218/DK 315 and formally named in 2003.
facts.quote: In 2003 the tooth (catalogued as MGUH 27218/DK 315 in the Geological Museum of Copenhagen) was made the holotype specimen of Dromaeosauroides bornholmensis—scientifically named and described by Christiansen and Bonde.

facts.statement: A second dromaeosaurid tooth was found by ranger Jens Kofoed in late summer 2008.
facts.quote: In late summer 2008, ranger Jens Kofoed found a second dromaeosaurid tooth.

facts.statement: The second tooth, specimen DK 559, was found in the same location and assigned to Dromaeosauroides.
facts.quote: This specimen (DK 559) was found in the same location, and later assigned to Dromaeosauroides as well.

facts.statement: The Natural History Museum of Denmark certified the second tooth as Danekræ and noted the animal would have been feathered.
facts.quote: In a press release, the second dromaeosaur tooth was also certified Danekræ by the Natural History Museum of Denmark, which compared the animal to the raptors in the film Jurassic Park, noting that the animals, unlike the film's raptors, would have been feathered.

facts.statement: In 2012, Jesper Milàn and colleagues described coprolites containing fish scales and bones from the Jydegaard Formation.
facts.quote: In 2012, Jesper Milàn and colleagues described two coprolites (fossilised faeces) containing fish scales and bones.

facts.statement: Marine turtles and dromaeosaurids like Dromaeosauroides are the most likely candidates for producing the fish-eating coprolites found.
facts.quote: Although the producer of these faeces cannot be identified with certainty, marine turtles and dromaeosaurids such as Dromaeosauroides are the most likely candidates.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen is a single tooth crown measuring 21.7 mm in length, 9.7 mm in width, and 6.6 mm at the base.
facts.quote: The holotype of D. bornholmensis is a tooth crown 21.7 mm long, 9.7 mm from front to back and 6.6 mm wide at the base.

facts.statement: The tooth features six square, chiseled denticles per millimeter along its cutting edges.
facts.quote: There are six denticles per millimeter (0.04 in), and each denticle is square and chiseled.

facts.statement: Based on a tooth roughly 25% larger than Dromaeosaurus teeth, the animal's body length was estimated at 3 meters or more, possibly reaching 4 meters.
facts.quote: The holotype tooth is roughly 25 percent larger than equivalent Dromaeosaurus teeth, from which a body length of 3 m or more was estimated for Dromaeosauroides; it may have been as long as 3 to 4 m.

facts.statement: Christiansen estimated the skull length at 35 cm and the total body weight at 40 kg.
facts.quote: In an interview, Christiansen estimated its skull to be 35 cm long and the animal's weight 40 kg

facts.statement: Flight was considered unlikely for an animal of this size, despite some smaller dromaeosaurs potentially being capable of flight.
facts.quote: Although some smaller dromaeosaurs may have been able to fly, flight was unlikely for an animal the size of Dromaeosauroides.

facts.statement: In 2003, Christiansen and Bonde classified it as a member of the Dromaeosaurinae subfamily within Dromaeosauridae due to similarities with Dromaeosaurus.
facts.quote: In 2003, Christiansen and Bonde classified Dromaeosauroides as a member of the Dromaeosaurinae subfamily within the Dromaeosauridae, due to its similarity to Dromaeosaurus.

facts.statement: It is not considered part of the genus Dromaeosaurus because the two lived 60 million years apart, with Dromaeosauroides in the Early Cretaceous and Dromaeosaurus in the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Dromaeosauroides is not considered part of that genus. It is unlikely that a genus would survive for 60 million years; Dromaeosauroides lived during the Early Cretaceous, and Dromaeosaurus during the Late Cretaceous.

facts.statement: In 2008, Johan Lindgren and colleagues considered it an indeterminate dromaeosaur.
facts.quote: Dromaeosauroides was considered an indeterminate dromaeosaur by Johan Lindgren and colleagues in 2008.

facts.statement: In 2010, Oliver W. M. Rauhut and colleagues suggested that similar teeth might belong to the tyrannosauroid Proceratosaurus rather than Dromaeosauroides.
facts.quote: Oliver W. M. Rauhut and colleagues cautioned in 2010 that theropod teeth from the Late Jurassic/Early Cretaceous similar to those of dromaeosaurids may instead have belonged to the small tyrannosauroid Proceratosaurus or related taxa.

facts.statement: In 2021, Nicholas R. Longrich and colleagues proposed that it may have been an early eudromaeosaur.
facts.quote: Nicholas R. Longrich and colleagues stated in 2021 that Dromaeosauroides may have been an early eudromaeosaur.

facts.statement: Milàn and colleagues speculated that it could have used its enlarged sickle claw for 'spear fishing' to catch fish like Lepidotes, based on coprolite evidence.
facts.quote: Based on possible dromaeosaur coprolites from the Jydegaard Formation, which contained scales of the fish Lepidotes, Milàn and colleagues speculated that some dromaeosaurids were able to catch fish with the enlarged sickle claw on the second digit of the foot, similar to the "spear fishing" that has been proposed for the theropod Baryonyx and its enlarged thumb claw.

facts.statement: A second known tooth was found, measuring 15 mm in length with features identical to the holotype.
facts.quote: The second known tooth is smaller—15 mm—with the same features as the holotype.

facts.statement: The development of deep snouts in dromaeosaurids was likely an adaptation for handling vertebrate prey.
facts.quote: The development of deep snouts in addition was probably an adaptation for handling vertebrate prey.

facts.statement: A 2011 study by Denver W. Fowler and colleagues suggested dromaeosaurid sickle-claws were used to grip and pin down prey like modern birds of prey, while the mouth was used for dismemberment.
facts.quote: A 2011 study by the palaeontologist Denver W. Fowler and colleagues found these ideas unlikely, and instead suggested the claws were used like those of modern birds of prey, to grip and pin down prey, and immobilise it while dismembering it with the mouth.

facts.statement: Dromaeosauroides lived during the Berriasian age, between 139.1 and 137.05 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Berriasian to Berriasian (139.1 to 137.05 million years ago)

facts.statement: Dromaeosauroides belongs to the family Dromaeosauridae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Dromaeosauridae

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Dromaeosauroides is Dromaeosauroides bornholmensis.
facts.quote: Type species: Dromaeosauroides bornholmensis

facts.statement: Remains of the Scandinavian-Russian Early Cretaceous fauna, including Dromaeosauroides, are found only in Bornholm and Scania.
facts.quote: Bornholm and Scania appear to be the only places were remains of the Scandinavian-Russian fauna of the Early Cretaceous can be found.
